title: Matches page paginates DB rows BEFORE applying client-side filters, producing incorrect counts and near-empty pages
evidence: dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/matches/page.tsx:227-289 — `.range(from, to)` runs first (`pageSize=25`), then JS filters out by `activeSearch`, `filterNoticeType`, `filterSetAside`, `filterState`, `filterNaics`, `filterMaxDeadlineDays`. The reported total is set to the filtered-page length (line 288: `setTotalCount(anyClientFilter ? filtered.length : (count || 0))`).
impact: When a user types a search term or picks a notice type/state/NAICS filter, the page often shows 0–3 rows even when thousands of matches exist. The 'Sort by deadline/agency/notice_type' buttons also only re-sort the current 25-row page, never the full set — so 'sort by deadline' will never surface the soonest deadline unless it happens to be on page 1.
recommendation: Push notice_type / set_aside / state / NAICS filters into the Supabase query as `.eq()` / `.like()` on `opportunities.<col>` (already using `!inner`, so this is one-line each). Move search to an RPC or use `.or()` against `opportunities.title.ilike` / `opportunities.agency.ilike`. Sort by deadline/agency/notice_type must go through `.order('opportunities(...)', ...)`. Only then `.range()`.

title: Pipeline weighted-value forecast reads only `award_amount`; ignores `estimated_value`, showing $0 for every Sources-Sought / forecast deal
evidence: dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/pipeline/page.tsx:131 selects `opportunities(..., award_amount, strategic_scoring)` but NOT `estimated_value`. The weighted-pipeline math at lines 291-300 (`sum + (opp?.award_amount || 0) * prob`) treats every deal without a finalized award as $0. The portal sibling at dashboard/src/app/(portal)/portal/pipeline/page.tsx:134 already selects `estimated_value` — they have drifted.
impact: Every pre-award deal (Sources Sought, RFI, presolicitation, custom deal entered by user) contributes $0 to the dashboard pipeline forecast. Total-pipeline KPI on the pipeline page systematically under-reports, hiding 6-figure deals from the founder's view.
recommendation: Add `estimated_value` to the SELECT at line 131 and 221, then change the sum to `(opp?.award_amount || opp?.estimated_value || estimateContractValue(opp))`. The `estimateContractValue` helper is already used on the opportunity detail page.

title: Opportunity detail page uses SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY for every render — bypasses RLS for `opportunities`, `contacts`, `bid_protests`
evidence: dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/opportunities/[id]/page.tsx:44-48 — `const supabaseKey = process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY || process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY; … createClient(supabaseUrl, supabaseKey)`. Then queries `opportunities`, `contacts`, `bid_protests` with this key. `academy/[slug]/page.tsx:121` does the same.
impact: These tables already have public-read RLS today, so nothing leaks _now_. But the page silently bypasses every future RLS policy you add (paywall enforcement, tier-based hide, per-user opp blocklist, GDPR delete). Any future change to lock down contact emails or bid_protests will be invisibly bypassed here.
recommendation: Replace with `createSupabaseServerClient()` (already used in dashboard/page.tsx and elsewhere) and drop the `SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY` fallback. If a specific cross-user read is genuinely needed, scope a server-only helper that explicitly comments why it's bypassing RLS.

title: Document/cap-statement uploads use `getPublicUrl()` — any URL holder can download the file forever
evidence: dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/documents/page.tsx:103 — `const { data: urlData } = supabase.storage.from("client-docs").getPublicUrl(path); … file_url: urlData.publicUrl`. Same pattern at dashboard/src/app/(portal)/portal/documents/page.tsx:99 and dashboard/src/app/(portal)/portal/messages/page.tsx:144. Path is predictable: `user-documents/{profileId}/{timestamp}-{filename}`.
impact: Capability statements, proposals, certifications, internal reference letters are accessible to anyone with the URL (which sits in the DB, gets emailed, shows in logs, may be shared via support). UEI guessing + timestamp brute force is feasible for targeted exfiltration. Violates the data-handling promise on the privacy page.
recommendation: Make the `client-docs` bucket private, store the `storage_path` only (no URL), and serve via a signed-URL endpoint (`createSignedUrl(path, 300)`) when the user clicks download. Migrate existing rows by stripping the public URL on read and re-signing.

title: Unauthenticated /api/engine/[action] runs `child_process.exec` on arbitrary action keys
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/engine/[action]/route.ts:8-44 — POST handler with NO auth, maps `action` param to a static script list and runs `execAsync(\`python3 "${scriptPath}"\`)`. No `assertAdmin()` or `guardCron()` anywhere in the file.
impact: Any anonymous caller can POST /api/engine/score (or any other key) and trigger heavy Python jobs. On Vercel `exec` won't fire (CLAUDE.md notes this), but the route still attempts shell exec, returns a 500 with `error.message` (information leak), and is dead attack surface. If ever deployed somewhere with Python on PATH, it's RCE on arbitrary mapped scripts.
recommendation: Delete the file entirely — CLAUDE.md says the equivalent `cron/enrich` already had `exec("python ...")` ripped out for the same reason. Same applies to `dashboard/src/app/api/enrich/[opportunityId]/route.ts` (also unauthenticated exec, line 1-40).

title: 8 cron routes silently lose auth when env vars unset (anti-pattern CLAUDE.md called out)
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/cron/ingest_sam/route.ts:76, score_matches/route.ts:49, bulk_enrich_ai/route.ts:36, bulk_enrich_descriptions/route.ts:44, enrich_apollo_contractors/route.ts:148, ingest_fpds_awards/route.ts:166, naics_stats_backfill/route.ts:37, db_cleanup/route.ts:137 — all use `if ((expectedCron || expectedSvc) && auth !== expectedCron && auth !== expectedSvc)`. When BOTH env vars are missing the guard short-circuits to false and every request is accepted. CLAUDE.md explicitly calls this out: "the duplicated inline pattern silently bypassed every cron when the env var was unset".
impact: Any deploy where `CRON_SECRET` and `SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY` are both absent (preview branches, migration windows, accidental rotation) exposes these crons to the public internet — they reach SAM.gov with paid keys, mass-write to opportunities, run `db_cleanup` (destructive!), and burn OpenAI tokens. Today both vars are set, but the pattern is exactly the one Phase-2 hardening was supposed to retire.
recommendation: Replace each handler's inline auth with the shared helper: `const denied = guardCron(req); if (denied) return denied;` from `@/lib/cron-auth`. That helper is fail-closed in prod (`NODE_ENV === "production"` && no `CRON_SECRET` returns 401). Same migration the rest of the cron routes already did.

title: POST /api/email/welcome lets anyone spam welcome emails to any address
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/email/welcome/route.ts:4-23 — accepts `{ email, company_name, user_profile_id }` from anonymous POST body, calls `sendWelcomeEmail` + `enqueueDripSequence` with caller-supplied email. Empty `catch {}` returns 500 with no details. No auth, no rate-limit, no captcha.
impact: Reputation attack: attacker triggers 10k welcome emails to victim addresses on your Resend domain, Resend bounces / spam complaints poison your sender reputation. Also enrolls victim into 90-day drip via `enqueueDripSequence`. Cost: paid Resend sends + drip queue spam.
recommendation: Either delete the route (this should be called inline from signup, not as a public API) or gate it: require auth, then look up the caller's actual email from session — never accept email from body. If kept as a callback, require a signed Stripe/Supabase webhook signature.

title: POST /api/lead-magnet/deliver trusts client-supplied email + LinkedIn metadata with no session verification
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/lead-magnet/deliver/route.ts:105-185 — comment says "called by /auth/callback after a successful linkedin_oidc exchange" but the handler never calls `sb.auth.getUser()` or verifies the Supabase session. It just trusts `body.email` and `body.user_metadata`, inserts to `marketing_leads`, pushes to HubSpot, enqueues lead-brief job, fires Meta CAPI.
impact: Anyone can craft a POST that injects arbitrary email + arbitrary `linkedin_verified=true`/`linkedin_email_verified=true` payloads into your CRM and lead-brief pipeline. Skews scoring, poisons `lead_quality`, sends Resend mail to victim addresses, and burns Apollo+OpenAI quota on bogus leads. Also lets attackers impersonate "verified" prospects to sales.
recommendation: At the top of POST: read the Supabase session via `createServerClient` + `sb.auth.getUser()`, then enforce `email === user.email` and `user.app_metadata.provider === 'linkedin_oidc'`. Reject otherwise. The `/auth/callback` page is server-rendered so it can forward cookies — keep them.

title: POST /api/analyze-company/upload-cap-statement: anonymous 10MB uploads to Supabase Storage
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/analyze-company/upload-cap-statement/route.ts:25-114 — handler accepts multipart/form-data with no auth check. Only gate is `analysis_id` existing in `company_analyses` (which is publicly enumerable since analysis IDs are exposed in the /check/[analysisId] URL). Uploads up to 10MB to `client-docs` bucket per request.
impact: Cost-spam attack: attacker grabs any analysis_id from a Quick Checker share link, fires unlimited 10MB uploads. Each lands in your Supabase Storage bucket forever, scoped under a path you have no policy to clean up. Also writes attacker-controlled content into `inferred_profile.cap_statement_text` (used downstream in OpenAI prompts → prompt-injection risk).
recommendation: Require auth, OR require a short-lived signed token issued by the /api/lead-magnet/confirm flow that bound the upload right to a single analysis_id + 5-min TTL. Also rate-limit per analysis_id (e.g. max 1 cap statement). Add a Supabase Storage policy that enforces the same path prefix.

title: POST /api/leads has no rate limit; each call hits Apollo + HubSpot + Resend + OpenAI (paid)
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/leads/route.ts:48-308 — public CORS-allowed endpoint. Per-request pipeline: insert row, Apollo `people/match` call (line 158), HubSpot `upsertHubSpotContact` (line 192), Resend send (line 237), Meta CAPI fire (line 264), and `enqueueLeadBrief` (line 293) which queues a downstream OpenAI run. No IP throttle, no captcha, no honeypot beyond `rejectFakeSubmission`.
impact: $$ burn: 1000 spam POSTs = 1000 Apollo lookups (~$$$), 1000 HubSpot contacts (counts toward HubSpot CRM seat caps), 1000 Resend sends (deliverability damage), 1000 lead-brief OpenAI jobs (~$$). All without ever putting a real lead in front of you. Marketing leads table grows unbounded.
recommendation: Add `protectCrawl` (already exists at `@/lib/crawl-protection`, used by `public/contractors`) with `maxPerMin: 5` keyed on IP. Also rate-limit per email — same `email + magnet` should be a no-op after first hit (`isDuplicate` already detects but still runs full pipeline). Cache the Apollo result for 7 days keyed on `email+company`.

title: POST /api/beta-invites/[token] accepts unverified auth_user_id from body
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/beta-invites/[token]/route.ts:50-72 — POST does `await req.json()` to read `auth_user_id`, then writes it directly to `beta_invites.claimed_by`. Never verifies that the caller's actual session matches `auth_user_id`.
impact: Attacker who knows a beta token can spoof `claimed_by` to be any user UUID. Lets them frame another user as the claimer (audit-log tampering) or steal a beta invite by claiming it under their own ID while keeping the token visible to the legitimate recipient. Worst case: re-claim every public invite token under a single attacker account.
recommendation: Read the auth_user_id from `sb.auth.getUser()` in this route — never trust the body. If the route is meant to be callable pre-signup (when no session exists), only allow `claimed_by = null` and have a separate authenticated endpoint that later patches `claimed_by` to the session user.

title: 32 tables have RLS enabled but ZERO policies → service-role-only; PostgREST returns empty on all reads
evidence: Supabase advisor `rls_enabled_no_policy` flags 32 tables: agencies, alert_autofixes, api_connectors, archive_types, attachment_analysis_jobs, backlink_agents/contacts/monitor/outreach/prospects/todos, beta_invites, cancellation_feedback, capture_outcomes, cron_runs, dod_contracts, email_events, gao_protests, government_contacts, health_alerts, internal_config, opportunity_types, past_performance_stats, pdf_extract_cache, reengage_sends, rss_sources, sec_prime_filings, socrata_sources, wage_determinations, _backfill_targets_federal_2026_06_08. Several of these are user-facing (government_contacts is 5,882 rows of decision-makers; agencies 2,939; beta_invites; cron_runs is queried by /admin/health). With RLS on + no policy, only service_role bypass works — every authenticated/anon SELECT silently returns 0 rows.
impact: Two failure modes coexist: (a) admin/portal pages that query through anon-key SDK get empty results and either render blank or fall back to service_role with the key shipped in code — a real data-leak path; (b) anything that DOES read via service_role becomes invisible to RLS and ships the entire table to anyone who can reach the endpoint. Either way: the security model is incoherent.
recommendation: For each table, decide intent: reference data (agencies, archive_types, opportunity_types, naics/psc_codes, rss_sources, socrata_sources, far_clauses_cache, federal_hierarchy, past_performance_stats, wage_determinations, federal_hierarchy) → add `CREATE POLICY <t>_read ON <t> FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (true)`. Server-only (cron_runs, alert_autofixes, health_alerts, worker telemetry, beta_invites, backlink_*, pdf_extract_cache, internal_config, attachment_analysis_jobs, api_connectors) → `REVOKE ALL FROM anon, authenticated` and leave service-only. User-scoped (government_contacts when surfaced per-user) needs a real predicate. Add an automated check in `tools/30_smoke_admin.mjs` that fails CI on `rls_enabled_no_policy`.

title: Public anon role can execute 6 SECURITY DEFINER RPCs including trigger_cron_route and purge_old_activity_log
evidence: Advisor `anon_security_definer_function_executable`: `compute_naics_market_stats(int)`, `enqueue_marketing_lead_apollo()`, `enqueue_marketing_leads_apollo_backfill(int)`, `purge_old_activity_log()`, `rls_auto_enable()`, `trigger_cron_route(text)` — all SECURITY DEFINER, all callable as anon via /rest/v1/rpc/. Migration 090_security_hardening.sql DID revoke EXECUTE from `trigger_cron_route`, `rls_auto_enable`, `purge_old_activity_log` (lines 25-27), but advisor still lists them — either a recreate after the revoke or the revoke never landed. The marketing-lead enqueue functions were never covered.
impact: Anonymous attacker can: (a) trigger any cron route by POSTing /rest/v1/rpc/trigger_cron_route with `{"route_path":"/api/cron/whatever"}` — bypasses CRON_SECRET; (b) wipe client_activity_log via purge_old_activity_log; (c) flood marketing_leads enrichment queue with backfill calls (compute cost). 090 was the intended fix but the lint is still firing — revoke is missing or got recreated.
recommendation: Run `REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.trigger_cron_route(text), public.rls_auto_enable(), public.purge_old_activity_log(), public.compute_naics_market_stats(integer), public.enqueue_marketing_lead_apollo(), public.enqueue_marketing_leads_apollo_backfill(integer) FROM anon, authenticated;` in a new migration. Better: switch to SECURITY INVOKER and require service-role JWT. Verify by re-running get_advisors after deploy.

title: company_analyses INSERT policy is `WITH CHECK (true)` — anonymous can spam analyses + harvest emails
evidence: Advisor `rls_policy_always_true`: policy `Allow anonymous insert on company_analyses` for INSERT to anon+authenticated has `with_check = true`. The table has 460 rows with jsonb columns `firmographics`, `inferred_profile`, `competitors`, `crawl_data`, `sam_data`, plus lead_captured_at + startup_pack_unlocked_at. No row-ownership constraint means the same anon can insert millions of bogus rows.
impact: (1) cost-DOS: every analysis fires the Quick Checker pipeline (OpenAI, SAM, Apollo). (2) data quality: lead funnel becomes unusable. (3) PII: anon-inserted rows mixed with real captured leads make exports leak.
recommendation: Replace policy with a per-IP rate-limited Edge Function or a JWT-bound `with_check (auth.uid() IS NOT NULL)` + an unauthenticated /api/leads/start endpoint that uses service role + Cloudflare turnstile. Minimum: add a `created_ip` column + `rate_limit_buckets` join in the policy.

title: worker_jobs queue is hopelessly backlogged — 44,049 pending + 14,036 failed, no archival
evidence: `SELECT status, count(*) FROM worker_jobs`: pending=44,049, done=17,585, failed=14,036, running=3. Oldest pending dates back 2026-05-26 (15 days). Per-task breakdown: `extract_keywords` 17,638 pending (never claimed?), `extract_structured_reqs_federal` 11,630 pending, `classify_naics` 12,971 pending, `analyze_attachments` 13,733 FAILED (88% of attempts). Table is 35 MB but growing every opportunity INSERT via fan-out trigger; never purged. No DELETE policy for `status IN ('done','failed') AND finished_at < now() - interval '7 days'`.
impact: (a) Backfill is dead — extract_keywords / classify_naics workers are not draining their queues; the priority cron `run_worker_jobs` likely doesn't pick them up. (b) analyze_attachments 88% failure rate means something fundamental is broken (likely PDF download or OCR call). (c) Table will hit 1M rows fast since new opps trigger 3-5 jobs each — at 80K opps + growth, you'll see queue table multiply 10x.
recommendation: Three fixes: (1) Add a `worker_jobs_cleanup` cron that DELETEs `status IN ('done') AND finished_at < now() - interval '7 days'` and archives failed to `worker_jobs_archive`. (2) Investigate why `extract_keywords` + `classify_naics` aren't being claimed — check `/api/cron/run_worker_jobs` task-type filter array. (3) Open the analyze_attachments error_message column (`SELECT error_message, count(*) FROM worker_jobs WHERE task_type='analyze_attachments' AND status='failed' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 5`) and fix root cause.

title: 0 ON DELETE policy on 15 foreign keys — broken cascades on user deletion
evidence: 15 FKs use default NO ACTION: `user_profiles.managed_by → user_profiles(id)`, `client_tasks.assigned_by`, `client_documents.uploaded_by`, `client_activity_log.actor_id`, `client_messages.user_profile_id` + `.opportunity_id`, `user_feedback.user_profile_id`, `email_templates.updated_by → auth.users(id)`, `gov_keywords.added_by_user_id → auth.users(id)`, `profile_members.invited_by → auth.users(id)`, `profile_invitations.invited_by → auth.users(id)`, `admin_opportunity_pushes.pushed_by_user_id → auth.users(id)`, `outreach_prospects.reviewed_by → auth.users(id)`, plus `opportunities.naics_code/psc_code → naics_codes/psc_codes(code)`.
impact: Deleting an auth user errors with FK violation (can't actually delete users — see `account_deletion_requests` table that's never been processed). Deleting a managed-client profile leaves orphaned tasks/documents. The naics/psc FK on opportunities NO ACTION means you can never deprecate a NAICS code without touching 78K rows.
recommendation: For audit columns (assigned_by, uploaded_by, actor_id, invited_by, updated_by, pushed_by_user_id, reviewed_by, added_by_user_id) → `ON DELETE SET NULL`. For ownership (managed_by, user_profile_id, opportunity_id) → `ON DELETE CASCADE` if soft-delete not used, else SET NULL + filter. For reference codes (naics_code, psc_code) → drop the FK or `ON DELETE SET NULL`. Migration: `ALTER TABLE x DROP CONSTRAINT y; ALTER TABLE x ADD CONSTRAINT y FOREIGN KEY (...) REFERENCES ... ON DELETE SET NULL;`

title: Duplicate migration numbers (4 collisions) — apply order is undefined
evidence: `ls supabase/migrations/`: `019_quick_checker_competitors` + `019_quick_checker_enhancements`, `039_beta_invites` + `039_contractors_usaspending`, `060_academy_videos` + `060_opportunities_attachable_view`, `062_govtribe_cache` + `062_quick_checker_lead_capture_and_startup_pack`. Supabase MCP `schema_migrations` shows real timestamps (e.g. 060_academy_videos = 20260424212352) so the remote ran them in timestamp order, but the local filesystem-ordered CLI would apply them lexically by filename — different order on fresh provision.
impact: A fresh local Supabase or staging env reproduces the schema in a different order than prod. If two 019s touch the same table (e.g. quick_checker_competitors + quick_checker_enhancements both touch `client_competitors`), the result diverges. CLAUDE.md says "current latest: 070" but real latest is 096 — devs are guessing the next number.

Then add `tools/check-migrations.sh`: `ls supabase/migrations | cut -d_ -f1 | sort | uniq -d` must exit empty. Update CLAUDE.md to say "next free under supabase/migrations — current latest 096".

title: Mixed user-identity columns: 36 tables use user_profile_id, 4 use auth_user_id, 2 use profile_id — CLAUDE.md flagged this caused a security bug
evidence: Information_schema: `auth_user_id` (uuid) appears in user_profiles, profile_members, team_members, account_deletion_requests. `user_profile_id` (uuid) appears in 36 tables. `profile_id` in profile_invitations, profile_members. CLAUDE.md "Phase 1 security hotfix" notes: "`cron-trigger` + `cron-runs` queried `user_profiles.user_id` (column doesn't exist) → \"Run now\" buttons in /admin/crons always 403'd" — this is the same family of bug. `slack_installations` has both `user_id text` AND `user_profile_id uuid`.
impact: Every new RLS policy or admin handler has to remember which column to use. Mistakes silently fail closed (deny everything) or open (the cron_runs bug). With 36 tables on user_profile_id and 4 on auth_user_id, joins between them require `user_profiles` as a bridge — a perf cost and a footgun.
recommendation: Document the rule explicitly in CLAUDE.md: "auth_user_id = uuid REFERENCES auth.users(id) — used ONLY by user_profiles + team membership. user_profile_id = uuid REFERENCES user_profiles(id) — used by EVERYTHING ELSE." Add a CI lint that fails on new tables with `user_id` (no prefix) or that introduce `auth_user_id` outside the membership tables. Rename `slack_installations.user_id` → `external_user_id text`.

title: analyze_attachments task type has 88% failure rate (13,733 failed / 15,540 attempted) — silent enrichment hole
evidence: worker_jobs status by task: `analyze_attachments` done=1,807, failed=13,733. That's 88% failure with no alerting hookup; health_alerts has 415 rows but none for this. CLAUDE.md (2026-04-16 section) says "`structured_requirements` empty on 94.7%" was the previous problem this was supposed to fix — it's still broken via a different vector. opportunity_attachments table has 6,196 rows but `requirements_extracted jsonb` is presumably mostly null.
impact: AI Proposal generation (which CLAUDE.md says requires capability_statement and uses structured_requirements for context) gets garbage input. Customers see hollow proposals. The investment in the OCR/attachment pipeline is yielding ~12% of expected value.
recommendation: Run `SELECT error_message, count(*) FROM worker_jobs WHERE task_type='analyze_attachments' AND status='failed' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 10` to bucket failure modes. Likely culprits: (a) sam.gov API key throttled (mig 128_sam_api_key_3 exists — third rotation?), (b) PDF download timeout (Vercel 300s), (c) gpt-4o-mini JSON-mode rejection on large attachments. Add a health_alert when daily failure rate > 50% for this task.

refutations: The 13,733 failed rows are largely a stale historical residue from a known, already-fixed root cause — not an ongoing silent enrichment hole. The team has actively addressed this exact failure mode in the last ~10 days: (1) Commit f8cf0206 "split attachment + struct-reqs lanes — kill priority inversion" created a dedicated drain route at /api/cron/run_worker_jobs_attachments that ONLY claims analyze_attachments at batch_size=3. (2) Commit 9e929569 "eliminate analyze_attachments overlap + reap-burn loop" tightened the per-invocation budget to 150s (<180s cron interval) so concurrent invocations cannot stack — the route's own header comment explicitly attributes "98% of last-24h failures" to that stacking+reap-burn loop and says it's now fixed. (3) Migration 130 (commit 9c993d20, June) bumped analyze_attachments priority from 4→8 and backfilled the 12,723-row pending backlog so it actually gets claimed, while preserving the source-tuned routing from migs 121-124. (4) Migration 119 added reap_stale_jobs() which automatically requeues or fails stuck "running" rows (the very mechanism the finding's failure count came from). The finding also misattributes downstream impact: structured_requirements is now populated through the source-tuned extract_structured_reqs_federal lane (priority 6), which runs independently of attachments — so even with attachment failures, federal opps still get structured reqs. The recommendation to add a health_alert on >50% daily failure rate IS reasonable (no such alert exists today), but that's an observability nit, not the "high severity, hollow proposals" framing the finding presents. The 88% number is a lifetime aggregate dominated by the pre-fix reap-burn window, not a current rate.

title: contractors hot path: 188M sequential-tuple-reads despite extensive index set — query patterns bypass them
evidence: pg_stat_user_tables.contractors: seq_scan=3,781 / seq_tup_read=188,694,857 (every seq_scan touches all 83K rows; ~50× table-scan-equivalent worth of reads) AND idx_scan=889,371 — so most queries are indexed but a meaningful tail is doing full scans. Likely candidates: (a) the Partners search route's keyword/state combo when keyword leads, (b) Apollo enrichment cron looking for un-enriched rows without a partial idx on `WHERE apollo_enriched = false`.
impact: Every full scan reads ~41 MB from disk + 9.1 MB index lookup waste. With 3,781 scans in the recent window, that's 155 GB of unnecessary IO. Page-load on /partners + /competitors is the visible symptom.
recommendation: Enable `pg_stat_statements`, identify top-N scanning queries, and add targeted partial indexes: e.g. `CREATE INDEX idx_contractors_unenriched ON contractors (last_enriched_at NULLS FIRST) WHERE apollo_enriched = false;`. Convert `ILIKE '%foo%'` searches to use the existing `contractors_fts_idx` (which has 0 scans currently — see other finding).

title: warm_cf_cookie bug: error message originates in Railway/VPS worker, NOT Vercel — premise of the bug report is wrong
evidence: The literal string 'strict CF tenant + FLARESOLVERR_URL not configured' exists in exactly ONE file: tools/playwright-worker/worker.js:358. It does NOT appear anywhere in dashboard/src/app/api/cron/run_worker_jobs/route.ts. Database query of failed warm_cf_cookie jobs over last 24h shows 93 occurrences of that exact message. Duration analysis: 68 of the 165 failures completed in <1s (consistent with the early-return path at worker.js:353-359 that fires BEFORE Chromium launches), and 72 took >30s (Playwright path). All originate in the worker.js process — Vercel does not have this code path. HTTP_TASK_TYPES in run_worker_jobs/route.ts:58-68 does not include warm_cf_cookie or scrape_portal_detail — Vercel never claims these jobs.
impact: The 'fix' the user is hunting for in Vercel env doesn't exist there. The real problem: the worker.js process (Railway or Hostinger VPS) DOES claim warm_cf_cookie jobs (proven by the error string), but its FLARESOLVERR_URL env var is empty at runtime even though the user believes they set it. Either (a) the worker was never restarted after the env change, (b) there are TWO worker processes and only one has the env, or (c) the user's claim that 'the VPS log only shows scrape_portal_detail' is from a filtered/wrong log view. Result is 93 burned attempts/day on Bonfire+OpenGov hosts that mark themselves blocked for 6h, killing all bid scraping on those tenants.

title: CATASTROPHIC: 42,000+ enrichment jobs starved for 14 days — extract_keywords + classify_naics had 0 consumed in 24h

title: analyze_attachments 82% failure rate over 7d (5,937 of 7,242) — all 'reaped after stuck running > 00:10:00'
evidence: Postgres: task_type='analyze_attachments' last 7d → 1,305 done / 5,937 failed = 82% failure rate. Last 24h: 907 done / 653 failed = 41.9%. Duration analysis of failed jobs: min=1,504s, avg=1,510s, max=1,628s — every single failure has duration ~25 minutes (timeout-then-reaped). Error message: 'reaped after stuck running > 00:10:00' (653 occurrences in 24h, the #1 error in the system). run_worker_jobs_attachments/route.ts sets maxDuration=300 and totalBudget=150_000 (line 50, 201), but successful jobs already average 38s with p95=1,512s — individual jobs exceed the 150s budget.
impact: Burning $$$ on Mistral OCR + LLM calls that never get attributed because the parent function dies at 300s, leaving the job 'running' until the reaper at 10min. The reaper increments attempts, the job re-enters the queue, gets re-claimed, and the whole cycle repeats. Multi-attachment opps may consume 5+ attempts × ~$0.05 LLM cost = ~$0.25/opp on jobs that produce no output. Federal opp pipeline degraded — opportunities show stale structured_requirements because the LLM enrichment pass is failing.
recommendation: 1) The per-link timeout in handleAnalyzeAttachments (run_worker_jobs/route.ts:595, run_worker_jobs_attachments/route.ts:96) is `if (Date.now() - start > 30_000) break` — but the LLM call after that has no timeout. Wrap callLLMJson in AbortSignal.timeout(60_000). 2) Add per-job hard limit: if Date.now() - jobStart > 100_000, finish_job(status='failed', error='per_job_timeout') BEFORE the next operation so the reaper never sees it. 3) Investigate the 1,628s max duration — that's 27min, which means the Vercel function ran way over its 300s maxDuration. Likely a hung fetch on a SAM.gov attachment that never aborts. Add AbortSignal.timeout(20_000) to the fetch at line 620 (currently only the second fetch has it). 4) Run a one-time UPDATE to mark all 5,937 failed-via-reap jobs as `status='failed', attempts=max_attempts` so they don't get retried again on the next reap cycle.

refutations: Finding is STALE — already fixed in commit 9e929569 ("fix(worker-queue): eliminate analyze_attachments overlap + reap-burn loop") deployed 2026-06-10 06:46 local (~12:46 UTC), several hours before this review. The commit message even cites the exact same data points the finding cites (653 failed / 576 done = 53% in 24h, 270s budget vs 180s cron overlap as root cause). Verified live in Supabase: since the fix deployed, analyze_attachments has 368 done / 0 failed. Last 1 hour: 103 done / 0 failed / 1 pending. The route now has budget=150s (< 180s cron interval, so no overlap), batch_size=3, JOB_BUDGET_GUARD=45s that re-releases unstarted jobs to 'pending' without burning attempts, and a watermark check (_analyzed_attachments_at in structured_requirements) that makes reaped+requeued jobs no-op when work was already done by an overlapping container. Both run_worker_jobs and run_worker_jobs_attachments handlers got the watermark check. The 7d aggregate the finding cites includes pre-fix data and is no longer representative of current behavior. Additionally, the finding's recommendation #1 (AbortSignal.timeout on callLLMJson) and #3 (AbortSignal.timeout on first fetch) were NOT the actual root cause — the root cause was Vercel cron invocation overlap, which the fix addressed at the orchestration layer, not the per-call layer. Recommendation #4 (bulk UPDATE stuck jobs to terminally failed) was not applied but is moot — the watermark check prevents wasted LLM calls on reaped+requeued opps.

title: playwright-worker leaking 230 zombie Chrome processes

recommendation: In dashboard/src/app/api/webhooks/resend/route.ts add: after eventType === 'bounced' || 'complained', INSERT INTO outreach_optouts (email, reason) VALUES (lower(recipient), 'resend:'||eventType) ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING. Then in dashboard/src/lib/email.ts send() add a pre-send check: SELECT 1 FROM outreach_optouts WHERE email=lower(to) — return false if found. title: email.ts send() wrapper has NO suppression check — every transactional/marketing path can email opted-out addresses
evidence: dashboard/src/lib/email.ts:163-196 send() checks isEmailEnabled(key) (a global category toggle) then calls r.emails.send() directly. recommendation: Add at start of send() in dashboard/src/lib/email.ts:163: `const { data: optout } = await sb.from('outreach_optouts').select('email').eq('email', to.toLowerCase()).maybeSingle(); if (optout) { console.log('[email] ' + to + ' opted out, skipping ' + key); return false; }`. title: process_scheduled_emails backlog: 286 pending rows, only 4 past-due — cron working but capability_statement template silently fails

title: /api/brand POST: no auth, no rate-limit, no hostname allowlist — full SSRF + cost-abuse vector
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/brand/route.ts:236-330: `POST` reads `website` from JSON body and pipes it directly into `fetch(url)` (line 246) AND `analyzeCompany("", url)` (line 256). There is no `getUser()`, no `protectCrawl`, no captcha, and no host validation. Worse, when `user_profile_id` is supplied in the body, the handler instantiates a SERVICE_KEY client (line 312) and writes `notes.brand_kit` to that profile id with no ownership check — any unauthenticated caller can clobber any user's brand_kit by guessing/leaking the UUID.
impact: (1) SSRF: attacker can probe internal IPs / metadata endpoints / private services via our egress IP. (2) Cost-abuse: each call fans out to Firecrawl + OpenAI + multiple HTTP requests with no throttle — a script can burn the OpenAI/Firecrawl budget in minutes. (3) IDOR write: any caller can overwrite any user_profile.notes.brand_kit (logo, colors, description) by guessing the UUID — corrupts client data.
recommendation: (a) Require an authenticated session via `createSupabaseServerClient` + `getUser()` and look up the caller's own profile id (ignore the body-supplied `user_profile_id`). (b) Wrap with `protectCrawl(req, { route: 'brand', maxPerMin: 5 })` so unauth burst-fetches die. (c) Before `fetch(url)`, resolve hostname with `dns.lookup`, reject any RFC1918 / loopback / link-local IP, reject non-http(s) protocols, and cap response size. (d) Drop the SERVICE_KEY write entirely — let the client persist via the regular `user_profiles` RLS-gated path.

title: /api/eligibility, /api/ai/write-proposal, /api/ai/draft-email, /api/ai/generate-proposal, /api/ai/draft-template, /api/ai/summarize-document — no auth, accept arbitrary user_profile_id (IDOR + OpenAI cost abuse)
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/eligibility/route.ts:17-35: POST accepts `user_profile_id` and `notice_id` from body, no `getUser()`, then `db.from('user_profiles').select(...).eq('id', user_profile_id).single()` returns the requested profile to the caller. Same pattern in dashboard/src/app/api/ai/write-proposal/route.ts:22-69 (loads profile by id, calls OpenAI for up to 10 pages of proposal text), dashboard/src/app/api/ai/draft-email/route.ts:23, dashboard/src/app/api/ai/generate-proposal/route.ts:27, dashboard/src/app/api/ai/draft-template/route.ts:22, dashboard/src/app/api/ai/summarize-document/route.ts:25.
impact: (1) IDOR read: anyone who guesses or learns any user_profile UUID can read company_name, naics_codes, sba_certifications, state, employee_count, revenue, federal_awards_count via /api/eligibility — that is the entire onboarding payload for every paying customer. (2) OpenAI cost-abuse: an unauth POST loop against `/api/ai/write-proposal` mints ~5K tokens per call; a few thousand calls drain the monthly budget and DoS legitimate proposal generation. (3) Outbound spam: `/api/ai/draft-email` returns finished outreach copy for any chosen POC — attacker can mass-generate phishing-ready emails on our credit.
recommendation: Add `const { data: { user } } = await createSupabaseServerClient().auth.getUser(); if (!user) return 401;` then resolve the caller's profile via `eq('auth_user_id', user.id)` and IGNORE any body-supplied `user_profile_id`. For routes that legitimately need to act on another id (admin-only), gate with `assertAdmin()`. Combine with per-user rate limit (e.g. 20 proposal generations / hour) backed by the existing `rl_bump` RPC.

title: /api/analyze-company (Quick Checker entry) has no rate-limit / captcha — cost-abuse + scraping vector
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/analyze-company/route.ts:1003-1080: anonymous POST takes a website URL, kicks off `crawler.analyzeCompany` (Firecrawl + multi-page crawl), SAM.gov entity lookup, Apollo enrichment, and an OpenAI run, then inserts into `company_analyses`. No `protectCrawl`, no captcha, no per-IP throttle. Logs only `x-forwarded-for`. The result is also returned in the response so it can be used as a free company-intel API.
impact: A script can submit 1000 websites/hour and (a) drain Firecrawl/OpenAI/Apollo/SAM budgets, (b) populate `company_analyses` with garbage rows that pollute the lead dashboard, (c) use CapturePilot as a free competitor-intel oracle.
recommendation: Wrap with `protectCrawl(req, { route: 'analyze-company', maxPerMin: 3 })`, add Cloudflare Turnstile/hCaptcha on the LP form, validate the `website` host (block RFC1918), and dedupe by `ip_hash + website` for 24h. Consider requiring an email-magnet token before the heavy crawl runs.

title: /api/leads has no rate-limit or captcha — lead-magnet form is wide open to enrichment + email-bombing abuse
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/leads/route.ts:48-280: POST accepts arbitrary email/name/company, runs Apollo enrichment (paid), upserts to HubSpot (CRM-pollution risk), and sends a Resend email containing the lead-magnet PDF — all unauthenticated. Only validation is `EMAIL_RE` regex + length caps. No HMAC/CSRF/captcha/per-IP throttle on the public surface.
impact: (1) Email-bombing: attacker submits victim@example.com 1000 times → Resend ships 1000 PDFs from CapturePilot domain, getting our sender domain blocked and burning Resend credits. (2) Apollo cost-abuse: every submit triggers a billable Apollo person-match. (3) HubSpot CRM-pollution: scripted submits fill the sales pipeline with junk contacts (each marked `lead_source_cp=lead_magnet`) — sales team has to triage.
recommendation: (a) Add `protectCrawl(req, { route: 'leads', maxPerMin: 2 })` keyed on IP hash. (b) Require Cloudflare Turnstile/hCaptcha token in the body, verified server-side before any work runs. (c) Dedupe by (email,magnet) within a 1-hour window — silently no-op repeats. (d) Move HubSpot+Apollo into a background job so a single submit can't fan-out paid calls before the throttle fires.

title: Public can EXECUTE 6 SECURITY DEFINER RPCs without signing in — including `trigger_cron_route` and `rls_auto_enable`
evidence: Supabase advisor `anon_security_definer_function_executable`: anon role can call /rest/v1/rpc/{compute_naics_market_stats, enqueue_marketing_lead_apollo, enqueue_marketing_leads_apollo_backfill, purge_old_activity_log, rls_auto_enable, trigger_cron_route}. `trigger_cron_route(route_path text)` lets the caller fire ANY cron route via the system; `rls_auto_enable()` likely toggles RLS state; `purge_old_activity_log()` can wipe the admin audit trail; `enqueue_marketing_lead_apollo` lets anyone burn Apollo credits.
impact: `trigger_cron_route` alone is catastrophic — an unauthenticated attacker can force-run any cron, including SAM ingest, scoring, email blasts, billing webhooks. `purge_old_activity_log` removes audit trails AFTER an incident. `rls_auto_enable` could enable/disable RLS on tables. `enqueue_marketing_leads_apollo_backfill(p_limit integer)` can drain Apollo budget at attacker-chosen rate.
recommendation: For each function: either `ALTER FUNCTION ... SECURITY INVOKER;` if RLS handles the gating, or `REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION ... FROM anon, authenticated;` and call only from server-side service-key clients. Add a migration that does both REVOKEs and re-grants only to the `service_role`. See https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/database-linter?lint=0028_anon_security_definer_function_executable

refutations: The finding is materially refuted by migration 090_security_hardening.sql, which already REVOKED execute on the three most dangerous functions called out: `trigger_cron_route(text)`, `rls_auto_enable()`, and `purge_old_activity_log()` — explicitly from both `anon` AND `authenticated`. Migration 090 was committed in 31af6469 ("sprints B/C/D/E/F: cron-fix + supabase-hardening"). The finding's headline impact ("trigger_cron_route alone is catastrophic — unauthenticated attacker can force-run any cron") is no longer accurate against the current codebase. Additionally: (a) `enqueue_marketing_lead_apollo` is a TRIGGER function (`returns trigger`) and PostgREST does NOT expose trigger functions via /rest/v1/rpc — it cannot be called by anon regardless of SECURITY DEFINER; (b) `compute_naics_market_stats(integer)` in migration 126 explicitly grants execute only to `service_role` (line 168), not anon. Only residual real exposure: `enqueue_marketing_leads_apollo_backfill(p_limit int)` was introduced in migration 118 (post-090) without REVOKE, so it inherits the public default grant. That function is rate-capped at p_limit (default 500) jobs and dedup-indexed, so an attacker can queue ≤500 Apollo enrichment jobs — minor budget burn, not catastrophic. The finding appears to be generated from a stale Supabase advisor snapshot taken BEFORE migration 090 was applied. As written (catastrophic, 3 fully-revoked functions cited, 1 trigger function falsely claimed as RPC-callable), the finding is not real in its current form.

title: 33 tables have RLS enabled but ZERO policies — silently locked or silently open depending on caller role
evidence: Supabase advisor `rls_enabled_no_policy` reports 33 tables in this state including `agencies`, `alert_autofixes`, `api_connectors`, `backlink_*` (8 tables), `beta_invites`, `cancellation_feedback`, `capture_outcomes`, `cron_runs`, `dod_contracts`, `email_events`, `gao_protests`, `government_contacts`, `health_alerts`, `internal_config`, `past_performance_stats`, `pdf_extract_cache`, `reengage_sends`, `rss_sources`, `sec_prime_filings`, `socrata_sources`, `wage_determinations`, `_backfill_targets_federal_2026_06_08`. For anon/authenticated roles, queries return empty. For SERVICE_KEY callers (every cron + every admin route), they return everything — masking the absence of authz logic.

Also: legitimate developers cannot see the table from the dashboard unless they switch to the service role, leading to confusion + accidental query against `auth.uid()` returning nothing in tests.
recommendation: Per table, either (a) add an explicit `CREATE POLICY ... FOR SELECT USING (false)` to make the intent explicit ("server-only"), or (b) add the right per-role policy. New migration `099_rls_policies_for_orphaned_tables.sql` should batch them. Document a convention in CLAUDE.md: every new RLS-enabled table must ship with at least one policy in the same migration.

title: HubSpot inbound webhook silently bypasses signature check when `HUBSPOT_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/hubspot/webhook/route.ts:28-31: `function verifyHubSpotSignature(req, rawBody): boolean { const secret = process.env.HUBSPOT_WEBHOOK_SECRET; if (!secret) return true; // Skip verification in dev if no secret configured ...}`. Same fail-open pattern that the 2026-05-22 cron-auth hardening was supposed to eliminate. If the env var ever drops in production (rotation, accidental unset, new Vercel env target), every webhook call is accepted and writes to `pipeline_activity` + `client_activity_log` + Supabase.
impact: Attacker who knows the URL (it's discoverable) can forge `contact.creation`, `deal.propertyChange`, `meeting.created` events — pollute the CRM pipeline, fake deal-stage moves, plant fake meeting log entries the team relies on for follow-ups.
recommendation: Mirror the `cron-auth.ts` pattern: `if (!secret) return process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`. In production, hard-fail with 500 if the secret is missing, log loudly, and return 401 to the caller. Add an `env-health` probe so the missing secret surfaces in /admin/health.

title: `/api/admin/impersonate` HMAC secret falls back to `SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY` then to literal string `"dev-secret"`
evidence: dashboard/src/app/api/admin/impersonate/route.ts:36-39: `function sign(payload): string { const secret = process.env.CRON_SECRET || process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY || "dev-secret"; return createHash('sha256').update(secret+'|'+payload).digest('hex').slice(0,32); }`. (1) Truncating to 32 hex chars (128 bits) is on the floor for HMAC. (2) Plain SHA-256 of `secret|payload` is not HMAC and is vulnerable to length-extension. (3) The `dev-secret` fallback means anyone in dev/staging who knows the source can forge an impersonation cookie for any user_profile_id and access the dashboard as that user.
impact: If `CRON_SECRET` and `SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY` are both unset (or in any preview/dev deploy that uses `dev-secret`), an attacker can encode `{a:'<any-uuid>', t:'<target-profile-id>', i:<now>}` + the known signature and present it as the `cp_admin_impersonate` cookie → instant account takeover of any tenant. Even with the secret set, length-extension on SHA-256 makes signature forgery feasible given any one known (payload, sig) pair.
recommendation: Switch to `crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(payload).digest('hex')` and compare with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. Drop the `dev-secret` fallback — fail-closed with `throw new Error('CRON_SECRET required')` in production. Add a startup assertion in the route module.

title: Signup says "No credit card required" but onboarding completion screen demands a card
evidence: dashboard/src/app/(public)/signup/page.tsx:210 — 'It\'s completely free right now. No credit card required.' Then dashboard/src/app/(onboarding)/onboard/page.tsx:633-639 — 'Last step: pick a plan to start your 14-day trial / Card required to unlock full features'.
impact: Classic bait-and-switch. A time-poor ops person who just spent 3-5 minutes typing in NAICS / firmographics hits a wall demanding their credit card. They'll either bounce (and feel deceived) or hit 'Just let me poke around first' — the tiny gray link at the bottom. Either way the funnel is leaking and trust is gone.
recommendation: Pick one truth. title: Sluggish dashboard load — KPI fetch is a single serial round-trip that can't render anything until /api/dashboard/kpis returns
evidence: dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/dashboard/DashboardClient.tsx:105-120 — entire dashboard hangs on one fetch to /api/dashboard/kpis. EMPTY_STATS shows 0 for every counter while loading. CLAUDE.md backlog: 'Overall dashboard speed — page loads are sluggish, needs profiling (likely waterfall Supabase queries that should parallelize)'. Plus the dashboard also synchronously waits on LiveOpportunityCount, DashboardMarketCard (per-NAICS fetch), SpendRadarCard, PipelineForecastCard, GovTribeActivityCard — each its own fetch on mount.
impact: User sees 'Welcome back, [company]' with all zeros, then a popcorn-storm of numbers settling 1-3 seconds later. Feels broken. On mobile/slow networks this is worse.
recommendation: Three changes: (1) Split /api/dashboard/kpis into the cheap counts (matches/pipeline) and the expensive aggregates (newOpps7d, recentPipeline, pendingActions) and stream them progressively. (2) Render skeleton numbers (animated bars) instead of '0' so zeros aren't briefly displayed. (3) Parallelize the card components — they all do their own fetch but mount serially because they're below the main stats fetch.
domain: CapturePilot 2.0 UX/UI audit — federal contractor perspective (onboarding, dashboard, portal, public/auth flows)

refutations: The finding is largely stale and misinterprets the architecture. (1) The "Overall dashboard speed — sluggish" CLAUDE.md backlog item was explicitly addressed in commit 296a8355 (May 29, 2026): "TTFB 10-20s → ~200ms by moving KPI queries off SSR critical path". The 2-stage render with skeletons WAS the fix. (2) /api/dashboard/kpis is not a "serial round-trip" — it batches 12 Supabase queries via Promise.all server-side, all using count: 'estimated' (O(1) pg_class.reltuples) instead of count: 'exact' to avoid the JOIN-and-walk problem. The route comment explicitly says "the page renders with skeletons immediately, KPIs stream in as this endpoint completes". (3) The claim that card components (DashboardMarketCard, SpendRadarCard, etc.) "mount serially because they're below the main stats fetch" is factually wrong — React renders the tree in one pass and all useEffect hooks fire in parallel; they're independent fetches. (4) EMPTY_STATS showing 0 during load is a minor polish issue (skeleton numbers would be nicer), not a "high severity performance" bug. The only valid sub-point — skeleton states instead of 0 — is cosmetic. The "high" severity label is wrong and most of the technical evidence misreads the code.

title: Four pairs of duplicate-numbered migration files
evidence: `ls supabase/migrations/` shows duplicate prefixes: 019_quick_checker_competitors.sql + 019_quick_checker_enhancements.sql; 039_beta_invites.sql + 039_contractors_usaspending.sql; 060_academy_videos.sql + 060_opportunities_attachable_view.sql; 062_govtribe_cache.sql + 062_quick_checker_lead_capture_and_startup_pack.sql. CLAUDE.md explicitly says 'pick the next free number'.
impact: Supabase CLI applies migrations in lexical order — duplicates load in non-deterministic order on a fresh DB, leading to potential schema drift between environments. Future renumbering breaks `supabase db reset` reproducibility.
recommendation: Rename the second of each pair to use the next free number with a `git mv` (e.g. 019_quick_checker_enhancements.sql → 020a_quick_checker_enhancements.sql with note, or shift everything above by one — risky on a deployed DB so prefer suffixing 019b/039b/060b/062b instead and update CLAUDE.md to record the convention). Re-run `npx supabase db diff` to confirm idempotency.
domain: Dead code, duplicate logic, and unused dependencies in dashboard/

refutations: The duplicate filenames physically exist, but the finding misrepresents both the impact and the recommended fix. dashboard/supabase/migrations/README.md explicitly documents all four pairs as "Known historical conflicts" that have shipped to prod, are frozen by design, and apply in deterministic alphabetical-by-suffix order. The recommendation to rename them (e.g. to 019b/039b/060b/062b) is exactly what the README warns against: Supabase tracks applied migrations by filename + content hash in supabase_migrations.schema_migrations, so renaming would either re-apply the SQL (breaking idempotency-unsafe statements) or hard-error with "migration already applied but contents changed", requiring manual DB intervention. The CLAUDE.md "pick next free number" rule already applies going forward — migrations 063-131 are all uniquely numbered, demonstrating the convention is being honored post-conflict. The impact claim of "non-deterministic order on a fresh DB / schema drift between environments" is wrong: alphabetical-by-suffix ordering is deterministic across Postgres tooling and the README confirms the current ordering works. The finding is essentially flagging a documented, accepted, intentionally-frozen historical artifact as if it were unaddressed tech debt.
